title: One by one
hook: Sariputta knew each state one by one as it arose
carry: each piece is small and passing

segments.voice: Yesterday: khandhas, five heaps and one monk's questions. Did you save a real question for the evening? Today, the Buddha talks about a student. Day four hundred eighty-four.

A sommelier tastes a wine and says: cherry, then leather, then something like pencil shavings. You taste the same glass and get: red. Wine. Same mouth, same sip. The difference is training: noticing things one at a time, in the order they come. The hundred and eleventh discourse opens with the Buddha praising someone. It isn't a king or a donor. It's his student Sariputta, and the praise is very specific. For half a month, the Buddha says, Sariputta saw his own mind's states one by one, as they came. Today: Anupada.
screen: `CHERRY, LEATHER, PENCIL SHAVINGS.` → `OR JUST: RED.` → `THE BUDDHA PRAISES SARIPUTTA.`

segments.voice: The discourse is called Anupada, which means one by one, in succession, step after step. The Buddha begins by calling Sariputta wise, with great wisdom, wide, quick and penetrating. Then he shows what that wisdom looked like in practice. Sariputta enters the first meditative absorption. Inside it, he doesn't just feel calm. He picks out what's there: applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, ease, a mind gathered to one point. Then contact, feeling, perception, intention, mind. Then zeal, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, attention. A long list, and he knows each one. And here's the key line, paraphrased: these states were known to him as they arose, known as they stayed, known as they passed. He saw that they hadn't been, and came to be. Having been, they vanished. So he wasn't attracted to them or repelled by them. He goes on this way through the deeper absorptions and the formless attainments. At the subtlest ones, where states can't be picked out as they happen, he looks back on them after he comes out. Why does this matter for someone who isn't a monk in deep absorption? Because an inner life can feel like one big weather system. I'm stressed. I'm fine. A meditator learns to see the parts: a tight jaw, a worried thought, a flicker of hope, a sound. Seen one at a time, each piece is small and passing. The Buddha ends by calling Sariputta his true son, born of the teaching, who keeps rolling the wheel the Buddha set turning. The praise is for a skill anyone can begin: seeing one thing, then the next.
screen: `ANUPADA: ONE BY ONE, IN ORDER` · `INSIDE CALM, NAMING EACH PART` · `ARISING, STAYING, PASSING` · `A TRUE SON, ROLLING THE WHEEL` · then, large: `ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: note states one by one. Sit and settle. When something shows up, give it one soft word: hearing. Itching. Planning. Calm. Doubt. Don't hunt for things, and don't fix them. Just name what comes, in the order it comes, and notice that each one, after a while, isn't there anymore. If you lose the thread, the first thing you notice when you come back is just the next one. The bell holds the time.
Anupada. The discourse where Sariputta is praised for seeing each state of his mind arise, stay and pass, one by one, step by step.
Your line: each piece is small and passing. Today, when a mood feels like a whole storm, find just one part of it, name it, and watch that part change. Day four hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: In insight meditation as taught in many Theravada centers, practitioners make light mental notes of what arises (hearing, thinking, feeling) one moment at a time, a method that draws on discourses like MN 111 and the foundations of mindfulness.

fork.setup: you're in deep calm, and pleasant states fill the mind. what did Sariputta do, according to MN 111?
options: hold on to them as long as possible.
know each one arising, staying and passing.
fork.reveal: he knew each one in turn, saw it come and go, and so was neither attracted nor repelled.

original.note: Pali anupada: step by step, one after another. the title of MN 111.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation is making the mind one blank, calm thing.
what it means: Sariputta's calm was full of parts, and he knew each one as it came and went.
what a scholar hears: MN 111 lists the factors of the first jhana in detail, a list later Abhidhamma texts expand into their analysis of mental factors.
recall: a lion's roar: a bold claim

notes: MN 111 paraphrased; the list of states in the first jhana is given in full order per the sutta as I recall it (vitakka, vicara, piti, sukha, cittekaggata, phassa, vedana, sanna, cetana, citta, chanda, adhimokkha, viriya, sati, upekkha, manasikara); confirm.
Half a month (addhamasa) as the period of Sariputta's insight: confirm.
The link to Abhidhamma mental factors in the trapdoor is a scholarly generalization; confirm wording.

Editor review (days 482–500): corrected the teach, which said Sariputta analyzed every attainment one by one 'all the way to the end'; in MN 111 he reviews the last two (neither-perception-nor-non-perception, cessation) only after emerging. Vitakka now 'applied thought'; removed a 'most of us' claim.
